content: In mathematics and logic, an operation refers to a specific action or procedure that generates a new value from one or more input values. Operations are categorized into two main types: unary and binary. Unary operations involve a single input value, such as negation or trigonometric functions. Binary operations, on the other hand, require two input values and include processes like addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and exponentiation. Operations are not limited to numerical values. For example, logical values such as true and false can be combined using logical operations like and, or, and not. Similarly, vectors can be added or subtracted, and rotations can be combined through function composition, where one rotation is performed followed by another. In set theory, operations include binary operations like union and intersection, as well as unary operations like complementation. Functions can also undergo operations such as composition and convolution. It is important to note that operations are not always defined for all possible input values. For instance, in the set of real numbers, division by zero is undefined, and square roots of negative numbers are not real. The set of input values for which an operation is defined is called its domain, while the set containing all possible output values is referred to as the codomain. The actual set of values produced by the operation is known as its range. For example, the squaring operation in real numbers produces only nonnegative values; thus, while the codomain is the set of all real numbers, the range is restricted to nonnegative numbers. Operations can also involve dissimilar objects. For instance, a vector can be multiplied by a scalar to produce another vector, and the inner product of two vectors results in a scalar. Operations may exhibit specific properties, such as being associative, commutative, anticommutative, or idempotent, among others. The input values involved in an operation are referred to as operands, arguments, or inputs, while the resulting value is called the output, result, or value. Operations can involve any number of inputs, not just two. An operation is conceptually similar to an operator, but the focus differs. For example, one might refer to the operation of addition or addition operation when emphasizing the operands and result, but use addition operator when focusing on the process or the abstract function it represents, such as ( + : S times S to S ). In general, an operation ( omega ) is defined as a function of the form ( omega : X_1 times dots times X_k to Y ). Here, the sets ( X_j ) are called the domains of the operation, ( Y ) is the codomain, and the fixed non-negative integer ( k ) (the number of arguments) is referred to as the arity or type of the operation. A unary operation has an arity of one, while a binary operation has an arity of two. An operation with an arity of zero, known as a nullary operation, is simply an element of the codomain ( Y ). An operation with arity ( k ) is called a ( k )-ary operation. Such operations are functional on their first ( k ) domains and are typically referred to as finitary operations, as they involve a finite number of arguments. Extensions of this concept allow for operations with infinite arity, such as those indexed by an ordinal, cardinal, or arbitrary set. Often, the term operation implies that the domain of the function is a Cartesian power of the codomain, although this is not universally the case, as demonstrated by the examples above.
